# 2 Maccabees Chapter 5 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 5 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_005_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Around this time Antiochus made his second invasion of Egypt.

**2** And it happened that throughout the city, for nearly forty days, there appeared in the air horsemen charging in golden gear and armed companies in full array of spears and swords —

**3** troops of cavalry drawn up, attacks and counterattacks on both sides, brandishings of shields, forests of spears, flights of arrows, flashes of golden ornaments, and armor of every kind.

**4** Therefore all men prayed that this apparition might prove to be a good omen.

**5** But when a false rumor arose that Antiochus had died, Jason took no fewer than a thousand men and made a sudden attack upon the city. When the forces on the wall were driven back and the city was being taken at last, Menelaus took refuge in the citadel.

**6** But Jason kept massacring his own citizens without mercy, not realizing that success against one's own kinsmen is the greatest of misfortunes, but supposing himself to be setting up trophies over enemies and not over fellow countrymen.

**7** He did not gain control of the government, however. In the end he got only disgrace from his conspiracy, and went again a fugitive into the country of the Ammonites.

**8** Finally he met a miserable end. Accused before Aretas the ruler of the Arabians, fleeing from city to city, pursued by all men, hated as a rebel against the laws, and abhorred as an executioner of his country and his fellow citizens, he was cast ashore in Egypt.

**9** And he who had driven many from their own country into exile died in exile, having embarked to go to the Lacedaemonians, in hope of finding protection there on account of their kinship.

**10** He who had cast out many to lie unburied had none to mourn for him; he had no funeral of any kind and no place in the sepulcher of his fathers.

**11** When news of what had happened reached the king, he took it to mean that Judea was in revolt. So raging in his mind he set out from Egypt and took the city by storm.

**12** And he commanded his soldiers to cut down without mercy those whom they met and to slay those who took refuge in their houses.

**13** There was a massacre of young men and old, a wiping out of women and children, a slaughter of virgins and infants.

**14** Within the space of three days, eighty thousand were destroyed, forty thousand in hand-to-hand combat, and as many sold into slavery as were slain.

**15** Not satisfied with this, he presumed to enter the most holy temple in all the world, guided by Menelaus, who had become a traitor both to the laws and to his fatherland.

**16** He took the sacred vessels with his polluted hands, and swept in with his profane hands what other kings had dedicated for the enhancement and glory and honor of the place.

**17** Antiochus was puffed up in mind, not perceiving that the LORD was angered for a little while on account of the sins of those who dwelt in the city, and that this was the reason he was indifferent to the holy place.

**18** But if it had not happened that they were involved in many sins, this man would have been scourged and turned back from his presumption as soon as he came forward, just as Heliodorus was, whom Seleucus the king sent to inspect the treasury.

**19** But God did not choose the nation for the sake of the holy place, but the place for the sake of the nation.

**20** Therefore the holy place itself shared in the misfortunes that befell the nation and afterward participated in its good fortunes; and what was forsaken in the wrath of the Almighty was restored again in full glory when the great LORD was reconciled.

**21** So Antiochus, having carried off from the temple eighteen hundred talents, hurried away to Antioch, thinking in his arrogance that he could make the land navigable and the sea passable on foot, so exalted was his mind.

**22** And he left governors to oppress the nation: at Jerusalem, Philip, a Phrygian by birth, and in character more barbarous than the man who appointed him;

**23** and at Gerizim, Andronicus; and besides these Menelaus, who lorded it over the citizens worse than the others. In his hatred for the Jewish citizens

**24** Antiochus sent Apollonius the Mysian, the commander of the Mysian mercenaries, with an army of twenty-two thousand, commanding him to slay all the grown men and to sell the women and the young.

**25** When this man arrived in Jerusalem, he pretended to be peaceably disposed and waited until the holy sabbath day; then, finding the Jews not at work, he ordered his men to parade under arms.

**26** He put to the sword all those who came out to see them, then rushed into the city with his armed men and killed great numbers of people.

**27** But Judas Maccabeus, with about nine others, withdrew into the desert and lived like the wild animals in the mountains along with his companions, feeding on what grew wild, so that they might not become partakers in the defilement.
